newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - ROYAL SAYS TO HIT MERGER TARGETS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ROYAL SAYS TO HIT MERGER TARGETS.

text.p: Royal & Sun Alliance said on Thursday it was confident of hitting its forecasts of 175 million pounds ($280.2 million) of annualised savings by 1998 for the six billion pound merger which created it last year.
Around 3,000 jobs have already gone and savings are currently running at some 95 million pounds chief executive Richard Gamble told Reuters.
He was speaking as the insurer reported an 11 percent rise in first half profits to 501 million pounds.
The recent strength of sterling took 25 million pounds off the headline figure.
But Gamble refused to be drawn on whether savings could exceed expectations.

"The 175 million pounds was blueprinted as the merger benefits by putting the two companies together. It's very difficult going forward to establish what additional savings are merger benefits," said Gamble.
"We'll deliver the 175 million pounds but we will be striving to reduce costs across all parts of our business. Like all businesses we're constantly trying to drive our cost base down."
Gamble pinpointed the UK and U.S. performance for the above market expectation results.
In the UK the group had spent a long time focusing on the core skills of underwriting and claims management both of which were prime features of the group's first half performance, he said.
But the rating environment remains difficult in the UK.
Personal motor insurance was the only area seeing a rise in rates and Royal Sun had put increases of 10 percent through in the last twelve months.
That had had a knock-on effect on exposures which were down 7 pct year-on-year but the company was prepared to let non-profitable business go, said Gamble.
Subsidence costs were another feature of the first half in the UK rising 19 million pounds to 56 million pounds as a result of the dry period between January and April.
Now a top ten player in UK life business Gamble said Royal Sun had the basis to be a major player in life business and certainly intended to do so.
But he was cautious about acquisitions.
"European life companies are extravagantly expensive and it would be very difficult in the current climate to justify an acquisition benefiting shareholders," he said.
"I'd never want to say that if the right opportunity came along we wouldn't be able to take it up but I have to say the focus is very much on completing the integration."

Royal Sun reaffirmed its commitment to the active management of its capital base but Gamble said a number of factor's needed to be taken into account when weighing up the possibility of further buybacks.
"We've set out our stall to buyback up to five percent of our shares and that's what we intend to do," he said.

"A major driver of the solvency figure is stockmarkets around the world - and they're booming. The question is can that last. Obviously we have to take that into account when looking at solvency and balance sheet strength."
The group has so far completed two percent of the repurchase.
Royal Sun had increased its exposure to equity markets over the last twelve months, he said, but of late had not made any major moves.

Responding to Wednesday's news that Britain's Personal Investment Authority (PIA) that the company had failed to meet the first deadline set in its pension misselling review Gamble insisted that was not the case.
"We set out our plan with the PIA, we met that plan, we delivered everything that we had said we'd deliver and now they're questioning it."
Gamble declined to give a figure for the provisions set aside to meet the costs of the review.
-- Simon Cowell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7721 ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
